name: Spanish
fwnote: Codes name the five goal areas (Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons, Communities) and their eleven standards as ACTFL numbers them (1.1–5.2), with the ACTFL proficiency range each unit targets; the alignment is the course author's judgment, not an ACTFL certification.

1.bq: How do the sounds of Spanish help you read any word out loud?
std: ACTFL 1.2
Interpretive mode: recognize and decode spoken and written Spanish sounds, syllables and first words at Novice Low.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: say and sing memorized words and short phrases (hola, adiós, the alphabet song) at Novice Low.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare the Spanish sound and spelling system (one vowel sound each, silent h, ñ, rr) with English.
1.write: Say or write 3 sentences in Spanish. Greet a friend, tell your name, and say goodbye. For example: ¡Hola! Me llamo Ana. ¡Adiós! Use your own name.
rooms: Five vowels that never change — the room

ch.bq: How can you read a Spanish word out loud the first time you see it?
ch.talk: Can you think of another name that reads the same from the end to the start?

l.look: Say mamá and papá. Does every a sound the same?
Sing the five sounds. Which one makes your lips round?
Sound out the word mesa, one letter at a time.
Read me the Spanish way. Now read no. Does no sound like English no?
Which word has the most claps? Clap it to check.
What do you say when you walk into class? What do you say when you leave?

ch.t: Special Letters: h, ll, ñ, rr
ch.bq: Which Spanish letters make sounds that English letters do not?
ch.talk: Which sound was harder for you, the ll in llama or the rr in perro?
ch.story: Yoyo and Perro at the Farm

s.t: The Quiet H and the J

l.look: Say helado without the h. Now say hola.
Say jugo. Then say hola. Which one has air at the start?
Say llama and pollo. Where do you hear the y sound?
Say año. Can you hear the ny sound in the middle?
Make your motor sound. Then say perro.
Which words need a rolled sound?

s.t: Say It Before You Know It

l.look: Say jirafa out loud. What animal is it?
How many more letters does Spanish have than English? Which one is it?

2.bq: How can we count and describe the things we see in Spanish?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: ask and answer ¿cuántos? and ¿de qué color es? with single words and short phrases at Novice Low/Mid.
ACTFL 1.2
Interpretive mode: understand numbers and color words in songs, games and pictures.
ACTFL 3.1
Connect to math and art by counting objects and mixing and naming colors in Spanish.
ACTFL 4.1
Notice that the color word follows the noun in Spanish, unlike English word order.
2.write: Draw a picture of your room. Then say or write 3 sentences in Spanish about it, like Hay tres libros. El libro es rojo. Use a number word, hay and a color word.
rooms: Colors and counting to twenty — the room

ch.bq: How can we count the things around us in Spanish?
ch.talk: What could you count in your classroom today, in Spanish?

l.look: Which word means three? Hold up that many fingers.
Count your toes in Spanish. Which word do you end on?
Which word means twelve? Say it out loud.
Ten blocks and nine blocks. What do you call that number in Spanish?
Count the windows in your room. Ask a friend, ¿Cuántas ventanas?
Say one thing that is in your room. Start with Hay.

ch.bq: How do we name the colors we see in Spanish?
ch.talk: What is your favorite color? Can you find something that color in the room?

l.look: Point to something red in your room. Say rojo.
What two colors make verde? Say them in Spanish.
Name something at home that is blanco.
Find something brown. Say its color two ways.
Which color has the most crayons? Say it in Spanish.
Say a red apple in Spanish. Put the color last.

3.bq: How do el and la help us name the people and things around us?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: point, ask ¿Qué es? and name family members, pets and classroom objects at Novice Low/Mid.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: present one's family with simple sentences such as Esta es mi mamá.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare Spanish noun gender and articles (el, la, un, una) with English, which has none.
3.write: Draw your family or your room. Label three people or things with el or la, like la mamá or el libro. Then say one sentence: Esta es mi... (This is my...).
rooms: El and la — naming what is here

ch.bq: How do we name the people and animals we love in Spanish?
ch.talk: Why do you think some tags say el and some say la?

l.look: Point to each person and say la mamá, el papá or el bebé.
Say the word for grandpa. Now change one letter to say grandma.
Point to each pet and say its name in Spanish.
Which pet do the most kids have? Say its name in Spanish.
Say each tag with el or la in front.
Draw your family. Point and say Esta es mi... for each person.

ch.t: Things in My Room and School
ch.bq: How can a word's last letter help us guess el or la?
ch.talk: Look at the words el libro and la mesa. What do you notice about the last letter?

l.look: Point to the book, the table and the chair. Say each word in Spanish.
How many pencils are in the backpack? Say the number in Spanish.
Point to a door and a window in your room. Say their names in Spanish.
Say the Spanish word for the bed, the book and the window.
Put each word in the el box or the la box. Use the last letter.
Point to a thing in your room. A friend asks ¿Qué es? You answer Es un... or Es una...

4.t: One and Many, Big and Little
4.bq: How do Spanish words change to show how many and what things are like?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: exchange simple descriptions and opposites (grande/pequeño, feliz/triste) with a partner.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: describe things with matching plural and adjective forms (los perros grandes) at Novice Mid.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare how Spanish marks plurals and adjective agreement on more than one word with English patterns.
4.write: Draw some animals. Label them or say 3 sentences in Spanish, like: Tres perros grandes. Una gata pequeña. Los gatos felices. Use a number, the thing, and a describing word that matches.
rooms: One and many, big and little

ch.bq: How do Spanish words change when there is more than one?
ch.talk: What do you have more than one of at home? How would you say it in Spanish?

l.look: One apple is la manzana. How do you say many apples?
Which row has no s at the end of perro? Why?
Say the plural of el tren and la flor out loud.
Try it yourself: what is the plural of luz?
Say the plural of el perro. Did you change both words?
Which words in the story go with las?

ch.bq: How do we tell what something is like in Spanish?
ch.talk: Who is big and who is little in the story? How did they feel at the end?

l.look: Name one thing in your room that is grande and one that is pequeño.
Who in your family is alto? Who is bajo?
Make a feliz face. Now make a triste face. Say each word.
How do you say the happy dog in Spanish?
How do you say the tall girl? Remember to match the -a.
Say the plural of la casa grande.

5.bq: What does it take to say a whole thought in Spanish, and to turn it into a no or a question?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: ask and answer yes/no questions and state likes with me gusta / no me gusta at Novice Mid.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: produce whole sentences with a subject and a conjugated -ar verb.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare Spanish verb endings that show the subject, and the ¿ mark, with English question and sentence patterns.
5.write: Escribe 4–6 oraciones sobre tu día o un juego. Write 4–6 Spanish sentences about your day or a game. Use at least three different people (yo, él or ella, nosotros), one sentence with no, one yes-or-no question, and one sentence with me gusta.
rooms: A whole thought in Spanish — the room

ch.bq: How can one small ending on a Spanish verb tell you who is doing the action?
ch.talk: Sofía left out the word yo in her last sentence. How could Grandpa still know who was talking?

l.look: In "Sofía camina," which word is the subject and which word is the verb?
Change "Marta canta" so it uses a pronoun instead of the name Marta.
Sofía says "nosotros" for her team. How many players on the field does that one word stand for?
Follow the same steps with cantar (to sing). What is the form for tú?
Chant the same five forms with bailar (to dance). What is the form for nosotros?
"Hablamos con el abuelo." Which pronoun is hiding in this sentence?
Find the -ar verb form canta in the saying. Who is the subject: I, you or he/she?
Tell Mamá that you and Leo walk to the park. Which form of caminar do you need?
Put these words in Spanish order: grande / canta / el perro. What sentence do you get?
Add up the rows. Do you get 20? Which part of the world has the most?

ch.bq: How do you turn a Spanish sentence into a no or a yes-or-no question?
ch.talk: Tomás answered "No, no canta." Why do you think he said no two times?

l.look: Make this sentence negative: "Tomás canta en la fiesta."
Ana asks you, "¿Bailas?" Answer that you do not dance, using the double no.
Write Tomás's answer to "¿Es gris?" as a full sentence that starts with yes.
Say "Caminas a la escuela" two ways: once as a statement and once as a question.
Write "Lucía, do you sing?" in Spanish with the marks in the right places.
Answer "¿Bailas en las fiestas?" in a full sentence about yourself.

s.t: A First Taste of Me Gusta

l.look: Which thing do the most students like? Say it as a sentence that starts with Me gusta.
How many friends said no? Say Ana's answer in Spanish.
Ask a partner if they like to sing. Then answer their question about you.
Think of an animal. Write three yes-or-no questions a friend could ask to guess it.

6.bq: Why does Spanish need two verbs for to be, and how do you know which one to use?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: exchange feelings, location and origin using ¿Cómo estás? and Soy de… at Novice Mid.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: describe oneself and a friend with ser (traits, nationality) and estar (feelings, place).
ACTFL 4.1
Compare Spanish's two verbs for to be with English's single verb.
6.write: Write 4 to 6 sentences in Spanish to introduce yourself to a pen pal. Say who you are and where you are from (ser), what you are like (ser), how you feel today (estar), and where you are right now (estar).
rooms: Soy and estoy — who I am, how I am

ch.t: Ser: Who and What I Am
ch.bq: How do you tell someone who you are, where you are from, and what you are like in Spanish?
ch.talk: Lucía used soy, es and somos. What do you think each one means, and how could you tell from the letter?

l.look: Say two sentences about yourself with soy: your name and one more thing.

l.t: Eres and Es: You, He, She
l.look: Point to three people in your room and say a sentence about each with soy, eres or es.
Cover the list. Can you say all five forms from memory, starting with yo soy?
How many students in this example class are from somewhere other than Chicago? Say one sentence with son de.
Say where you or someone in your family is from with a nationality word. Is it -o, -a or neither?
Ask a partner ¿De dónde eres? and answer in a full sentence.
Answer ¿Cómo eres? with two describing words that match you.
Say the job of two people you know with es and the right -o or -a ending.
Write three sentences about a friend: who, where from, and what they are like.

ch.t: Estar: How and Where I Am
ch.bq: How do you tell someone how you feel and where you are, and how do you choose between ser and estar?
ch.talk: Diego felt happy, then nervous, then tired. Why might Spanish use a special verb for feelings that change during a day?
ch.story: A Day at the County Fair

l.t: Estoy: How I Am Right Now
l.look: How do you feel right now? Say one sentence that starts with Estoy.
Say all five forms aloud. Which three have an accent mark?
Act out this talk with a partner. Change the feelings to match how you really are.
Which feeling has the most students in this example? Say it with Diez estudiantes están…
Why does Diego y Sara take -os even though Sara is a girl?
How many students in this example are not at school? Say one sentence with están en.
Pick an object in your room. Ask a partner ¿Dónde está…? and have them answer with aquí, allí or en.
Write two sentences about yourself: one with soy and one with estoy. Explain why each one fits.
Make up one more sentence about Rosa and ask a partner to choose es or está.

7.bq: How do questions help us get to know people and find out what we need?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: interview a classmate with question words and answer in full sentences at Novice Mid.
ACTFL 1.2
Interpretive mode: listen for the question word to understand what information is being asked for.
ACTFL 2.1
Use courtesy expressions (por favor, gracias, perdón) and relate these everyday practices to the cultural values behind them.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare the written accent on question words and ¿por qué? versus porque with English.
7.write: Escribe una entrevista. Write 4–6 lines in Spanish: a greeting, three or four questions with different question words (like ¿Cómo te llamas?, ¿Dónde vives?, ¿Cuántos años tienes?) with a full-sentence answer to each, and a polite thank-you at the end.

ch.bq: How does one small word at the front of a question tell you what kind of answer to give?
ch.talk: Which question word helped Lupe the most, and what answer did it give her?
ch.story: The Case of the Last Empanada

l.look: Point to a classmate and ask a partner ¿Quién es? Your partner answers with Es and the name.
Hold up something from your desk. Ask a partner ¿Qué es? and have your partner answer Es un… or Es una…
Ask a partner ¿Cómo es tu casa? or ¿Cómo es tu mascota? Answer with Es and two describing words.
Hide a pencil. Your partner asks ¿Dónde está el lápiz? Answer with Está en… and a place.
Answer in Spanish: ¿Cuándo es el Día de la Independencia de México? Start with Es el…
Ask ¿Cuánto cuestan dos empanadas y un jugo? Add the example prices and answer in Spanish.
Ask a partner ¿Por qué estás contento? or ¿Por qué estás cansado? Your partner answers with Porque…

l.t: The Accent That Marks a Question
l.look: Write two sentences: one with ¿Qué…? and one with que. Circle the accent in the question.
Take the sentence Lupe lee en la biblioteca. Make two questions from it with different question words.

ch.bq: What makes a conversation work when you ask good questions and give full answers?
ch.talk: Which polite words did the reporters use, and how did they help the interview go well?

l.look: Turn to a partner. Ask ¿Cómo te llamas? and answer with Me llamo. Then say Mucho gusto.
Say each age in a full Spanish sentence, like Marisol tiene nueve años. Who is the oldest?
Ask a partner ¿Dónde vives? Answer with Vivo en and your town or neighborhood.
Your partner asks three quick questions. Before you answer each one, say the question word you heard.
Answer in a full sentence: ¿Tienes una mascota? ¿Hablas español? Change each verb ending to -o.
Have a four-line talk with a partner. Each time you answer, add ¿Y tú?

s.t: Polite Words for a Good Interview

l.look: Ask a partner for a pencil in Spanish with por favor. When you get it, say muchas gracias.
Act out the hallway scene with a partner. Use perdón, gracias and de nada.
Use this plan to interview a partner. Write each answer as a full sentence about them, like Se llama Ana.

8.t: First, Then, Last: Telling a Day
8.bq: How do we tell a day or a story in Spanish so that a listener can follow every step?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: tell a partner about one's daily routine, days and times using sequence words.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: write and read aloud a short sequenced story or comic strip of four to six sentences at Novice Mid.
ACTFL 3.1
Connect to ELA by applying beginning-middle-end structure and connectors to a Spanish narrative.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare how Spanish tells time (Es la una, Son las tres) with English patterns.
8.write: Escribe un cuento corto: Mi día. Write 4 to 6 Spanish sentences about one day. Tell what you do in order with primero, luego, después and finalmente. Include one time (Es la una or a las tres) and join two ideas with y, pero or también.
rooms: First, then, last — telling a day

ch.bq: How can a few small Spanish words turn a list of actions into a day someone can follow?
ch.talk: Sofía used primero, luego, después and finalmente. Which of those words would you use to tell the first thing you do each morning?
ch.story: A Day with Sofía in San Juan

s.t: Words That Put Things in Order

l.look: Tell two things you do in the morning. Start one with primero and the other with luego.
Tell the last two things you do at night. Use después and finalmente.
Put the four sentences in the right order and read them aloud.

s.t: Times of Day and Days of the Week

l.look: Say one thing you do por la mañana, one por la tarde and one por la noche.
Which day is number 3? Which two days make the weekend?
Tell what you do on two different days. Start each sentence with el or los and a day.
Say three sentences about your day using como, voy and leo.
Ask a partner ¿Qué hora es? and answer for one o'clock.
At what time does Sofía go to school? Say it in Spanish: Voy a la escuela a las…

ch.bq: What makes a short story in Spanish easy for a reader to follow from beginning to end?
ch.talk: What is the beginning, the middle and the end of Marco's story? Say each part in one short sentence.

l.look: Join these two sentences with y: Leo un libro. Como una manzana.
Finish this sentence with pero: Me gusta la pizza, pero…
Tell one thing you do, then add a second matching thing with también.
Tell a tiny story about a lost toy in three sentences: a beginning, a middle and an end.
Write a four-sentence story about a day at the park. Use at least two order words.
Plan a four-box comic about your morning. Write one short Spanish sentence for each box.
Fix this sentence: Marco juego con su perro.
Describe your own backpack or bag in Spanish. Check that the endings match.
Read your own story aloud. Where can you join two sentences with y, pero or también?

9.bq: How do the first words we say to someone show who we are and how much we respect them?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: greet, introduce, spell one's name and ask ¿De dónde eres? at Novice Mid/High.
ACTFL 2.1
Relate greeting customs, tú/usted choices and the two-surname naming practice to the perspectives on respect and family behind them.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare letter names and accent marks that change meaning (papá/papa) with English spelling.
ACTFL 4.2
Compare formal and informal address and greeting customs with those of one's own culture.
9.write: Escribe un párrafo: preséntate a una persona nueva. In Spanish, write 5 to 7 sentences. Greet the person for the time of day, say your name and spell it, say where you are from and your nationality, introduce a friend with te presento a or le presento a, and say goodbye.

ch.bq: How does the way you say hello and goodbye show respect for the person in front of you?
ch.talk: Tomás talked one way to Daniela and another way to Señor Ramírez. Why do you think he changed how he spoke?

l.look: At 10:00 a.m. you meet your principal. Which greeting fits, and why?
Write your own day with three greetings. Pick a time, a place and a person for each one.
Act out this dialogue with a partner. Then change it so one person is tired and answers differently.
How are you today? Answer in Spanish with one of the four words and ask a partner back.
You leave a taquería after lunch. Write a two-line goodbye between you and the cook.
Why does Sofía skip chao with her teacher? Write one goodbye for a friend and one for a teacher.
Choose a goodbye for your coach after practice on Friday, when you meet again on Monday. Explain your choice.
Ask your grandmother and your best friend how they are. Write each question and underline the verb.
How do people greet each other in your family? Compare it with the scene above.

l.t: Te Presento a… and Mucho Gusto
l.look: Introduce a friend to your coach, then to your sister. Which words change, and why?

ch.bq: What can a person's name, and the way they spell it, tell you about who they are and where they come from?
ch.talk: Why might it matter to Valentina that people use both of her last names and spell them with the accent?
ch.story: A Name with Two Last Names

l.look: How many letters does Spanish have in all, and which one does English lack?
Spell your first name aloud with Spanish letter names. Which letters were the hardest?
Spell the last name of someone in your family aloud, including capitals and accents.
Write the question you would ask a new classmate and the one you would ask the new principal.
A father is Carlos Pérez Luna and a mother is Elena Castro Díaz. Their son is named Andrés. What is his full name?
Write a polite hello to an adult in your building, using a title and the right last name.
Answer ¿De dónde eres? for yourself, and add where one person in your family is from.
Add the rows. Do they make 20? Which region has the most Spanish-speaking countries?
Your friend Elena is from Perú. Write one sentence saying her nationality.
Write one sentence that uses both tú and tu correctly.

10.bq: How do numbers, clocks and calendars in Spanish help us plan, buy and celebrate together?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: exchange ages, prices, phone numbers, times and dates at Novice Mid/High.
ACTFL 1.2
Interpretive mode: understand spoken numbers, clock times and day-first dates.
ACTFL 2.1
Relate how holidays such as Día de los Muertos and Mexican Independence Day are celebrated to the perspectives they express.
ACTFL 3.1
Connect to math by doing arithmetic aloud in Spanish (más, menos, son).
ACTFL 4.1
Compare Spanish conventions (day-first dates, lowercase months, tener for age) with English.
10.write: Write an invitation in Spanish (5–7 sentences) to a party or event. Say what it is, the day and date (el … de …), the time with de la mañana, tarde or noche, how much any tickets or food cost, and how old the birthday person is if it is a birthday.

ch.bq: How can a small set of number words build every number from zero to a thousand?
ch.talk: Marisol heard treinta, y and cinco and put them together. What other big numbers could you build from small number words you already know?
ch.story: Five Hundred Pesos at the Mercado

l.look: Which number words from once to quince sound a little like their English partners, and which do not?
Build 27 and 18 the same way. Which one needs veinti- and which needs dieci-?
Which two tens start with the same three letters, s-e-s and s-e-t? Say each one three times.
Say the numbers from 99 to 105 out loud. Where does cien change to ciento?
Find the three hundreds whose first part does not match the small number word. How are they different?
Say the year you were born in Spanish, piece by piece.
Say 400 chairs (la silla) and 400 books (el libro). What changes?
Marisol buys mangos and the yo-yo. Say the total in Spanish. How much is left from 500 pesos?
Which number did Ana get wrong, and why is that pair easy to mix up?
Write two sentences about the ages of people in your family, or of made-up characters.
You pay 200 pesos for something that costs 145 (example price). Say the subtraction in Spanish.

ch.bq: How do Spanish speakers say when something happens, from the hour on the clock to the day on the calendar?
ch.talk: Diego almost read 12/10 as December tenth. What could go wrong if you mix up day-first and month-first dates on a real trip?

l.look: Why does the answer change from son las to es la at one o'clock?
Which two rows use a word instead of a number for the minutes?
Use the three steps to say 11:45 and 3:55 in Spanish.
Say each departure time with de la mañana, de la tarde or de la noche.
Which sentences tell about something that happens every week, and which about one day only? How can you tell?
Which month is the one with twenty-eight days? What happens to it in a leap year?
Write today's date the Spanish way, in numbers and in words.
Answer the teacher's question with your own birthday, in a full Spanish sentence.
Which items on this ofrenda show that the family is remembering a specific person?
Say each date in Spanish with el … de …. Which one uses el primero?

11.bq: How do small words like el, la, hay and tengo help you describe and survive your school world in Spanish?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: manage classroom talk, ask for help (¿Cómo se dice? ¿Puede repetir?) and say what one needs at Novice Mid/High.
ACTFL 1.2
Interpretive mode: understand classroom commands and questions about what is in a place.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare noun gender and number patterns, including Greek -ma words and exceptions, with English.
11.write: Escribe un párrafo sobre tu clase de español (Write a paragraph about your Spanish class). Include what there is in the room (hay), two things you need (necesito), two things you have (tengo), and one class and its time.

ch.bq: How can a word's ending tell you whether to say el or la, and how do you make it plural?
ch.talk: Why do you think Lupe knew el mapa was right even though the word ends in -a? How do heritage speakers learn gender without rules?
ch.story: A Room Full of Sticky Notes

l.look: Say each noun out loud with its article three times. Which family has more nouns ending in -o?
Make the plural with the right article: el escritorio, la puerta.
Find every indefinite article in the dialogue. Is each noun masculine or feminine?
Use the pattern: el or la for bandera (flag) and armario (cabinet)?
Guess the Spanish word and its article for celebration and activity.
Write labels with el or los for: programa, sistemas, clima.
Find el día, la mano and la foto in the scene. Which ones break the -o/-a pattern?
How would you label yourself: el estudiante or la estudiante? Which word would describe your teacher?
Which noun on the list needed -es instead of -s? How many chairs are there for each table?
Make the plural: el pez (the fish) and la nuez (the nut).
Fix this label: los libro nuevos (the new books).

ch.bq: What Spanish do you need to get through the first week of school, from your supply list to asking for help?
ch.talk: Sofía was nervous about asking the teacher to repeat. Why is asking for help a language skill, not a weakness?
ch.story: The First Week at a New School

l.look: Describe your own classroom in three sentences that start with Hay or No hay.

l.t: Hay With Un, Una or Numbers
l.look: Fix this sentence two ways: Hay el mapa en la pared.
Ask and answer in Spanish: ¿Cuántos lápices hay? ¿Cuántas carpetas hay?

s.t: What I Need and What I Have

l.look: Tell a partner two things you need for school and one thing you need to do tonight.
Ask a classmate if they have three different school supplies, using ¿Tienes…?
Sofía needs tres cuadernos and dos carpetas. How much do they cost together at these example prices?
Write your own schedule in Spanish with the article for each class.
Ask a partner what time two of their classes are, and answer about yours.
Take turns giving three class commands to your group. Can they act each one out?
Pick the lifeline you would use if you know the word ruler in English but not in Spanish. Say the full question.

12.bq: How do Spanish speakers describe who someone is, how they are right now, and how they compare to others?
std: ACTFL 1.1
Interpersonal mode: compare people and things using más/menos… que in conversation.
ACTFL 1.3
Presentational mode: describe a family member or famous person in appearance and personality at Novice High.
ACTFL 4.1
Compare ser/estar meaning shifts and adjective placement and agreement with English usage.
12.write: Escribe un párrafo sobre una persona importante en tu vida. Write a paragraph in Spanish (6–8 sentences) that says who the person is and where they are from, describes their looks and personality, tells how they are or where they are today, and includes one comparison with más… que, menos… que, mayor or menor.

ch.bq: How can one English verb, to be, need two Spanish verbs, and how do you choose the right one?
ch.talk: Think of one thing about you that is always true and one thing that is true only today. Which one would use ser and which would use estar?
ch.story: Two Cousins at the Same Party

l.look: Find every form of ser in the dialogue and name its subject. Then introduce yourself with two sentences using soy.
List every form of estar in the texts and write its subject. Then write a text telling a friend where you are right now.

List every preterite and every imperfect. For sabía, funcionaba and dijo, explain in one phrase why that tense fits.
Underline the stem each verb pair shares, and say what changed between the two versions and what did not.
For each sentence name the trigger family (wish, judgment, emotion, doubt) and write the indicative form the verb was built from.
Try the routine on decir, ser and saber. Which one gives the same form for two different verbs, and how does context tell them apart?
Fill each blank and write the question that decided it: when, finished or background, or trigger. Compare answers with a partner and argue any disagreement.
Which sentence changed the second fact to make the connector work? Which one uses the subjunctive, and what does that verb add to the meaning?
Find the two connectors that promise a relationship the sentences do not have, and replace each with a better one or with nothing.
Find the five errors, name the family each belongs to, and rewrite the paragraph. Which error did you spot last, and why?
Which sentence has both a connector and a subjunctive? Explain what para que does to the verb after it.
Which pass found the most errors, and why might reading backward explain that? What does the reading-aloud pass find that the others miss?

ch.bq: How do you build, deliver and defend a five-minute talk in Spanish that an audience will remember?
ch.talk: Lucía's thesis fit on one index card. Why might a thesis you can say in one breath be easier to defend than a paragraph you have memorized?

s.t: Choosing a Topic and a Thesis

l.t: A Topic You Can Stand Behind
l.look: Finish the third step for the soccer example and write a step 3 for two more topics: la comida and las fiestas.
Which thesis is the easiest to attack, and what would a skeptic say? Rewrite it so it is narrower.
Lucía uses only the first row in her talk. Which other row would most surprise her audience, and how could she say it in one Spanish sentence with según?
Which card has the least written on it, and why does that not matter? Add one transition to card 2 that would introduce the coquí story as evidence.
Name the three moves in Ending B. What does Ending A make the audience feel about the talk they just heard?
Add the rows and confirm they total 300 seconds. Why does the third reason get the most time, and where would you cut first if a rehearsal ran long?
Read the third version aloud, holding each slash for one second and the double slash for two. Where would you look up?
Answer each in the three-step shape. Which question should get an honest I do not have that figure, and how would you say it?
Say what is wrong with A and with B. Then rewrite C for a teacher, changing every tú form to usted.
A student with flawless grammar but no evidence and no transitions might score 4, 1, 4, 3, 2. What is the total, and which two rows should that student work on first?
Which comment points to a grammar error, and what rule does it name? Rewrite the Presentación comment using sugiero que instead of te recomiendo que.
